strengths: Large-scale synthetic HDR dataset (24,000 images) addresses a critical bottleneck—~200x larger than existing datasets, solving the limited real-world data problem
Well-designed rendering pipeline with thoughtful technical choices (linear color space, floating-point storage, camera shake simulation) demonstrating engineering quality
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies, cross-dataset generalization tests, and evaluation on both labeled/unlabeled data with multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, HDR-VDP2)
Consistent and significant improvements demonstrated across multiple architectures and test sets (e.g., 2dB gain on Challenge123 PSNR-µ), with strong visual results showing artifact reduction
Thorough dataset analysis with quantitative diversity metrics and t-SNE visualization demonstrating superior coverage compared to existing datasets
Practical, plug-and-play domain adaptation method that works across CNN and Transformer architectures with zero inference overhead via re-parameterization
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, appendices, and promised code/dataset release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: adapter design closely follows VIDA [24] and LoRA [14] without substantial HDR-specific adaptations; test-time adaptation uses standard mean-teacher framework; uncertainty-based scale adjustment (Eq. 2) is overly simplistic without principled justification
Significant domain gap remains (Figs. 2, A1) in texture-rich regions despite sophisticated rendering; insufficient analysis of gap causes or solutions to address remaining mismatches
Missing critical ablations: no data scaling study to isolate quality vs. quantity benefits; no ablation on rendering parameters; no analysis of which scenarios contribute most to improvement

Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; marginal improvements on some metrics (SSIM <0.002); very small test sets (27-36 samples) raise generalization concerns
No comparison with alternative domain adaptation methods—only compares against baselines trained on real data, not other adaptation strategies, preventing assessment of adapter optimality
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: rank values (rs=1, rt=64) and augmentation parameters borrowed without HDR-specific validation; no sensitivity analysis provided

Rendering validation gaps: no quantitative comparison of rendered vs. real sensor characteristics; limited analysis of camera shake effectiveness; unclear if rendering detail matches actual camera properties
Computational overhead of test-time adaptation not analyzed; requires N forward passes but inference cost not reported despite practical deployment concerns
Limited evaluation scope: only two small real-world test datasets; no evaluation on diverse camera sensors or extreme scenarios; unclear generalization to other HDR applications
Evaluation limited to two datasets with significant domain-specific characteristics; lacks broader real-world validation beyond SCT and Challenge123

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: 24,000 HDR images, 6x larger than prior work, addresses real data scarcity in HDR fusion
Thoughtful dataset design with careful rendering pipeline preserving linear HDR format, diverse motion types, lighting conditions, and realistic imperfections like camera shake
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablations, multiple real-world datasets, both CNN and Transformer architectures, and quantitative diversity metrics
Well-executed work with clear presentation, extensive supplementary material, and systematic evaluation protocols
Both labeled and unlabeled domain adaptation scenarios with no inference overhead
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: S2R-Adapter directly applies existing LoRA-based methods [24] with straightforward share/transfer branch design; no theoretical justification for this decomposition in HDR context
Marginal empirical improvements: 0.6-0.7 dB on SCT and 2 dB on Challenge123 (27 test samples) are within noise margins; gains on Challenge123 much larger suggests potential overfitting
Substantial synthetic-to-real domain gap persists: 7.66 dB PSNR-µ gap between S2R-HDR-only training and real data (Table 4); Figure 2 shows separated distributions after adaptation
Fine-tuning on real data still required for SOTA, undermining practical utility when real-world annotation is needed anyway; unclear advantage over simpler baseline approaches
Weak ablations: share branch alone (43.32 dB) nearly matches both branches (43.33 dB); transfer branch alone is worse (43.20 dB); learned scale factors add only 0.01 dB benefit (Table 5)

Limited evaluation scope: only two small real-world datasets (Challenge123 has 27 test samples); no user studies to validate visual quality claims; missing comparisons with alternative domain adaptation methods
No analysis of dataset design choices: which components (camera shake, noise levels, scene types) actually improve downstream performance? Arbitrary choice of 1000 × 24 frame sequences unjustified
Unclear primary contribution: conflates dataset and method contributions; if dataset is main value, the adapter's added value is marginal; if method is main focus, improvements are insufficient
Reproducibility concerns: promised dataset/code links missing; training details vague (specific layer injection indices, rank selection rationale); no user study validation
Missing ablations: no comparison of dataset size effects, domain randomization alternatives, evaluation on additional datasets (Kalantari, Real-HDRV only in appendix), or analysis of failure modes

strengths: Addresses critical data bottleneck: 24,000 images is 166-270x larger than prior HDR datasets (89-144 samples), solving a genuine limitation in the field

Carefully engineered dataset design: custom UE5 rendering pipeline avoids tone mapping artifacts, linear HDR format enables flexible augmentation, diverse scenarios (indoor/outdoor, multiple times of day, varied motion types)
Quantitatively validated dataset diversity: 7-metric analysis (Table 1) demonstrates superiority over real datasets in extent of HDR, intra-frame diversity, and overall style

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple baselines (CNN and Transformer), multiple real datasets (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Real-HDRV), extensive ablations, both labeled and unlabeled scenarios

Consistent strong results: state-of-the-art on benchmarks (0.6-2.0 dB improvements in PSNR-µ), effective generalization to unseen datasets without ground truth labels, improvements across architectures

Well-designed domain adaptation: two-branch structure thoughtfully separates knowledge sharing (low-rank) and transfer (high-rank), zero inference overhead via re-parameterization, uncertainty-based scaling principled
High reproducibility and presentation quality: promise to release dataset and code, clear implementation details, comprehensive supplementary material, well-organized writing
Significant practical value: dataset addresses challenges mentioned in introduction (large motion, extreme dynamic range), architecture-agnostic method applicable to CNNs and Transformers
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: S2R-Adapter closely follows existing work (VIDA [24]), uses standard mean-teacher framework and uncertainty-based scaling; core contribution is application not algorithmic innovation

Insufficient analysis of strong generalization: paper shows models trained on S2R-HDR generalize well to real domains they haven't seen, but provides limited explanation for why; deeper analysis of learned representations or task-specific properties would strengthen understanding

Small test sets limit statistical validity: primary benchmarks have only 27-36 test samples; no confidence intervals or significance testing; some improvements (0.6-0.7 dB) may be within noise; missing error analysis of failure modes

Arbitrary dataset design parameters: many choices lack validation - camera shake percentage (30%), specific noise levels (σ ∈ [0.0001, 0.001]), metric selection (why these 7?); no ablations on individual design contributions (e.g., impact of camera shake in isolation)

Dataset diversity analysis has limitations: 7-metric approach somewhat arbitrary, t-SNE visualization can be misleading, task-specific diversity analysis missing, no assessment of synthetic data biases (unrealistic lighting distributions, object distributions)

Test-time adaptation details underspecified: N augmentations required but sensitivity to N not explored, claimed 'no computational overhead' but actual TTA cost not detailed, missing comparison with simpler adaptation baselines or standard fine-tuning

Limited application scope validation: introduction mentions computational photography, visual perception, autonomous driving, but experiments only validate standard HDR fusion benchmarks; generalization claims broader than demonstrated

Domain gap explanation superficial: while domain gap visualized (Figs. 2, A1), explanation of texture differences in specific regions doesn't deeply address why the adapter is needed or what specifically transfers; missing quantitative domain gap metrics
Missing comparison baselines: no comparison with domain randomization, adversarial adaptation, or simple fine-tuning; limited analysis of individual component contributions to adapter performance
Ethical considerations unaddressed: no discussion of potential biases in synthetic data, systematic failure modes from rendering-only training, or robustness guarantees for real-world deployment

strengths: Large-scale, high-quality synthetic HDR dataset (24,000 images) that substantially exceeds prior work and addresses a real bottleneck in the field
Thoughtfully designed rendering pipeline with careful attention to realistic synthesis, including tone mapping, camera shake, and multiple auxiliary outputs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations, multiple datasets, multiple metrics, and both supervised and unsupervised adaptation scenarios
Strong empirical improvements on synthetic benchmarks (6+ dB on SCT) demonstrating dataset effectiveness
Clear presentation with good visualizations of dataset diversity and domain gap analysis
Full reproducibility with publicly available code and dataset
Solid technical execution and proper experimental methodology throughout
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - S2R-Adapter applies straightforward existing adapter designs (shared/transfer branches) without significant innovation
Modest improvements on real-world datasets (0.4-0.6 dB on Challenge123), contradicting claims of 'state-of-the-art' performance and suggesting the domain gap problem is not fully solved
Weak evidence for domain adaptation effectiveness - t-SNE visualizations show visible cluster separation, indicating the shared branch may not fully capture domain-invariant features
Insufficient analysis of what dataset characteristics drive improvements - lacks deeper insight beyond 'larger scale and more diversity'
Uncertainty-based scale factor adjustment (Eq. 2) appears ad-hoc and lacks thorough justification or validation of the specific formulation
Test-time adaptation adds 0.23 seconds per image overhead, limiting practical applicability for video/batch processing
Limited comparison with alternative domain adaptation methods - primarily compares against simple fine-tuning rather than other domain adaptation strategies
No ablation or justification for key design choices (e.g., low-rank vs. full-rank projections, specific rank selections)
Lacks analysis of failure cases and limitations of the proposed approach
Camera motion synthesis validation missing - synthesized Perlin noise motion distributions not validated against real-world characteristics

strengths: Large-scale, high-quality synthetic HDR dataset with 24,000 images and careful rendering design appropriate for HDR fusion tasks
Comprehensive and diverse dataset covering indoor/outdoor environments, multiple lighting conditions, and various motion types
Extensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (SCT, Challenge123, Kalanari) with thorough ablation studies and supplementary analyses
Well-documented reproducibility with promised code/dataset release and detailed implementation specifications in appendices
Thoughtful rendering pipeline with proper tone mapping, gamma correction, and camera shake simulation for realistic synthesis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of domain adaptation method - S2R-Adapter combines standard low-rank decomposition and high-rank adapters with simple scalar scaling, lacking sophistication compared to recent adapter literature

Modest experimental improvements (0.6dB on SCT, 2dB on Challenge123 PSNR-µ) with questionable practical significance; models trained solely on S2R-HDR still substantially underperform real-world trained models

Weak domain gap analysis - t-SNE visualizations and difference maps are superficial; lacks rigorous investigation into which rendering components cause domain misalignment and how they affect fusion quality
Misleading claims about computational cost and state-of-the-art performance; TTA adds 61% inference overhead (Table 17) contradicting 'no extra cost' claim
Insufficient analysis of when domain adaptation helps - no characterization of which scene types, lighting conditions, or motion patterns benefit from synthetic pretraining
Unfair experimental comparisons - mixed dataset training (S2R-HDR + real) versus pure real data training; baselines not adapted with domain adaptation strategies

Dataset limitations inadequately discussed - human diversity limited to predefined motion capture libraries, restricted animal/vehicle categories, no ethical considerations despite generalization claims
Paper unfocused - attempts to simultaneously contribute dataset creation, adaptation method, and multiple task applications, diluting core message and impact

strengths: Addresses a critical and practical need in HDR fusion research by providing the first large-scale (24,000 images) high-quality synthetic HDR dataset with comprehensive diversity in scenes, lighting conditions, and motion types
Sophisticated rendering pipeline using Unreal Engine 5 with proper tone mapping, gamma correction, and precise control over environmental factors, producing realistic HDR images suitable for training

Well-designed domain adaptation method (S2R-Adapter) that effectively bridges the synthetic-to-real gap through a principled two-branch architecture (shared and transfer branches) with uncertainty-aware scaling

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantiarn, Sen's, Tursun's) with consistent improvements (0.6dB on SCT, 2dB on Challenge123) and ablation studies validating each component
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation descriptions, promised code/dataset release, multiple evaluation metrics, and clear methodology suitable for community use

Strong generalization results showing that models trained on S2R-HDR outperform those trained on smaller real-world datasets, with clear visual improvements in artifact reduction and highlight recovery
High-quality presentation with clear motivation, excellent visualizations demonstrating both quantitative improvements and qualitative visual quality gains
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty - the two-branch adapter uses standard domain adaptation techniques (low-rank shared branch and high-rank transfer branch) with simple learnable scaling factors, making the core contribution primarily engineering-focused rather than algorithmic

Insufficient analysis of the synthetic-to-real domain gap - while difference maps and t-SNE visualizations are provided, systematic quantitative characterization of what specific texture, material, or lighting properties cause divergence is lacking

Test-time adaptation introduces 0.23 second overhead per image (Table 17), which is non-trivial for real-time applications, with limited discussion of implications or potential computational optimizations

Limited exploration of design choices and alternatives - no comparison with other rendering engines, limited justification for Unreal Engine 5 selection, and insufficient ablation on specific rendering parameter impacts

Motion and dynamic object diversity could be expanded - most examples show person/camera motion with limited exploration of complex multi-object interactions, occlusions, and natural dynamic scene variations
Dataset contributions limited to HDR fusion task - no exploration of generalization to related problems (image denoising, super-resolution, depth estimation), limiting broader impact potential

Incomplete discussion of failure cases and limitations - limited analysis of scenarios where synthetic data doesn't improve performance and which real-world characteristics are well vs. poorly represented
